awd_titl_txt: Conference: Advancing translational impacts through bilingualism and individual differences research
awd_abstract_narration:
Many people grow up using more than one language, but scientists and technology have not fully considered the wide range of ways that people learn and use language across the lifespan. This project brings together researchers to explore how people differ in their language experiences and abilities, and how those differences shape learning, thinking, and communication. By studying this variation, the project helps build more effective tools for education, health, and technology. A central activity of the project is a national symposium that brings together experts to share new ideas, including advanced statistical techniques and modeling approaches that better reflect the complexity of human language behavior. Other potential benefits include improved learning environments, more accurate assessments, and smarter technologies that benefit people with a broad range of language and cognitive profiles.

This project contributes to innovation in artificial intelligence (AI) and translational research. Current language-based AI systems often fail to capture the flexibility and complexity of real-world language use, especially when people shift between different communicative settings. By focusing on individual variation in language processing, the project will provide participants with tools to model neural and behavioral data in ways that improve the scientific accuracy of AI systems. These same approaches also enhance clinical and educational applications, such as the development of diagnostic tools, personalized learning support, and frameworks for identifying communication challenges. The outcomes of this project advance knowledge in ways that can be applied across many sectors, leading to more efficient services, reduced costs, and better outcomes across education, healthcare, and technology sectors.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This award supported the BRIDGES Symposium on Individual Differences in Bilingualism, held May 7–8, 2026, at St. John’s University in Queens, New York. The purpose of the project was to strengthen connections between scientific research on bilingualism and its applications in education, communication, and clinical practice.

Bilingualism is often described as a simple distinction between people who are bilingual and those who are not. In practice, bilingual individuals differ widely in when and how they learned their languages, how proficient they are in each language, how frequently and in what settings they use them, and how language relates to their upbringing. These differences can affect research findings and their application. The symposium therefore focused on how researchers can represent bilingual experiences more accurately and how this knowledge can inform work with bilingual students, families, and communities.

More than 150 researchers, practitioners, and students attended the symposium in person or online across 10 US States and three countries. The two-day program included two keynote lectures, three interdisciplinary panel sessions, two student poster sessions, and networking opportunities. More than 20 invited speakers represented psychology, education, linguistics, communication sciences, and clinical research. Presentations addressed bilingual language development, cognition and social understanding, mental health, clinical assessment, and teaching in dual-language settings. Keynote speakers Gigi Luk of McGill University and Wilma Bucci of Adelphi University connected research on bilingualism with educational and clinical questions.

The project advanced knowledge by bringing together theoretical, methodological, and applied perspectives that are often considered separately. Discussions highlighted the limitations of treating bilingualism as a single, uniform experience and emphasized the need for more precise measurement of language history, proficiency, language use, and social context. The symposium also identified the importance of including individual variation when interpreting research and translating findings into educational or clinical recommendations. These exchanges helped define priorities for future interdisciplinary research and research-to-practice collaboration.

The project’s broader impacts included expanding access to current bilingualism research and supporting the development of students and early-career researchers. Registration was free, and online participation made selected content accessible beyond the local region. Professional continuing-education opportunities were available for educators and speech-language professionals. More than 30 students presented posters on topics including language awareness, perspective-taking, trauma processing, bicultural identity, and media use. Five students received travel awards that enabled them to present their work and interact with established scholars.

The symposium also strengthened connections among researchers, educators, clinicians, students, and academic departments at St. John’s University and other institutions. By hosting the event in Queens—one of the most linguistically diverse communities in the United States—the project connected scientific questions about bilingualism with communities most directly affected by this work. Overall, the award promoted a more accurate, inclusive, and practically useful approach to understanding bilingualism while expanding opportunities for training, interdisciplinary exchange, and future collaboration.
